meta.title: The Locked Listening Booth
meta.author: QM Connect Workshop
meta.objective: Identify musical eras from stylistic evidence and describe music using core musical elements.
meta.brandFooter: Built with LearnAIID. AI-assisted, human-driven learning.

narrative.premise: The library's listening booth locked itself after a software update, with your playlist for tomorrow's exam still inside. The booth's assistant will release the door to anyone who can prove they listen like a musician: place a piece in its era, put the eras themselves in order, and describe what you hear in the language of the discipline.
narrative.successCondition: The booth unlocks when the listening is proven. There is no clock; music has never cared what time it is.

levels.title: The Booth
levels.brief: Three panels glow on the booth door: a mystery piece described but unnamed, a timeline with its eras scrambled, and an empty listening journal. DJ-9, the booth's assistant, has already filled in its own answers. It would like you to know it has excellent taste.

companionLines.text: I have identified the mystery piece already: sweeping, emotional, clearly Romantic. Confidence: 93.7%. You may skip to the journal.
companionLines.tell: The description DJ-9 read names a harpsichord playing continuo, terraced dynamics, and a single steady mood. Every one of those is Baroque evidence. DJ-9 matched the word 'expressive' to the era with the biggest reputation for feelings instead of listening to the clues.

challenges.prompt: The mystery piece: a harpsichord plays continuous accompaniment beneath an ornamented violin melody. The volume shifts in sudden steps rather than gradual swells, and a single affect holds from first bar to last. Which era is this?
hints: Do not ask which era the piece feels like. Ask which era built instruments and habits like these.
One instrument in the description had essentially retired from orchestras by 1800.
Sudden steps of loud and soft have a name, and the name has an era attached to it.

options.feedback: Correct. Harpsichord continuo, ornamented melody, terraced dynamics, and a single sustained affect are the Baroque fingerprint. You identified it from evidence, which is the whole skill.

Romantic music swells and recedes gradually, and by then the harpsichord had been replaced by the piano for nearly a century. This is DJ-9's answer, reached by matching mood words instead of evidence.
Twentieth-century music tends to break the very conventions this piece follows faithfully: functional harmony, steady affect, continuo texture. Nothing here is being broken.

challenges.prompt: The booth's timeline panel has shuffled the eras. Put them back in chronological order, earliest first.
hints: Two of these eras are named for rebirth and for ornament; rebirth comes first.
The era of powdered wigs and balanced phrases sits between ornament and emotion.
Chant is oldest. Feeling-forward is most recent of the five.
challenges.keyboardInstructions: Select an era, then use the up and down arrow keys to move it. Press Enter to drop it in place. Your position is announced after every move.
challenges.explanation: Medieval, Renaissance, Baroque, Classical, Romantic. Each era pushed against the one before it, which is why the order is the story: polyphony blooming out of chant, ornament out of balance, feeling out of form.

challenges.prompt: The listening journal is empty. Describe the mystery piece in two or three sentences using at least three musical elements by name: for example melody, rhythm, dynamics, texture, or timbre.
hints: Name the element, then say what the music does with it. 'The dynamics shift in sudden steps' beats 'it gets loud.'
The description on the door panel already handed you observations for three elements. Translate them into your own sentences.
A reader who has never heard the piece should be able to imagine it from your journal entry.

rubric.criterion: Names at least three musical elements
rubric.lookFor: Three element terms used correctly: melody, rhythm, dynamics, texture, timbre, harmony, form.
rubric.commonMiss: Describing feelings ('it sounds fancy') without naming any element.

rubric.criterion: Ties each element to an observation
rubric.lookFor: Each named element comes with what the music actually does: ornamented melody, terraced dynamics, continuo texture.
rubric.commonMiss: Listing element names with no description attached to them.

challenges.exemplarAnswer: The melody is highly ornamented, carried by a violin over a steady harpsichord continuo, so the texture keeps a clear top line above constant accompaniment. The dynamics move in terraced steps rather than gradual swells, and the timbre of the harpsichord gives the whole piece a bright, plucked edge.

levels.evidenceFragment: The Booth: the era was in the evidence, not the mood. DJ-9 matched a feeling to a reputation; you matched instruments and dynamics to a century.
levels.unlockText: The booth door slides open, and your playlist is exactly where you left it. Somewhere in its circuits, DJ-9 quietly revises its confidence.

finale.title: The Door
finale.setup: Era identified from evidence, timeline restored, journal written in the language of the discipline.
finale.prompt: Before the booth lets you go: what is one piece of stylistic evidence you will listen for on the exam that you would have missed a week ago?

rubric.lookFor: A specific listenable feature: continuo, terraced dynamics, ornamentation, an instrument's timbre.
Says what the evidence points to, not just that it exists.

finale.closingText: The booth unlocks. Not because you named the piece; because you could show your listening.
